title: Machine-learning tremor catalog reveals Japan Trench spatial and slow-slip relationships
summary: A machine-learning monitoring system applied to eight years of S-net seafloor records detected seven times more tectonic tremors than the previous envelope-correlation catalog. The denser catalog resolved tremor activity extending along strike and dip, tremor patterns synchronized with slow-slip events, higher tremor energy rates near large-earthquake asperities, and a positive relationship between energy rate and recurrence interval; authors interpret the latter as evidence consistent with plate-boundary frictional heterogeneity.
ai_technology: DiET convolutional neural network and GrASP graph-based station association, with hybrid envelope-correlation/energy-ratio hypocenter location
organization: Geological Survey of Japan, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology; Tohoku University

evidence.tested: A machine-learning monitoring system applied to eight years of S-net seafloor records detected seven times more tectonic tremors than the previous envelope-correlation catalog.
evidence.unknown: The paper reports a substantial catalog expansion and interprets energy-rate patterns as suggestive of frictional heterogeneity; this is not a prospective earthquake forecast or proof of a causal friction mechanism. The abstract states prior work had already observed complementary tremor/earthquake distributions in the region, so the new contribution is the expanded catalog and improved resolution of the relationships, not the first observation of any complementary distribution.
evidence.ai_role: The CNN classified station spectrograms as earthquake, tremor or noise; graph clustering associated station detections, enabling a higher-resolution catalog from continuous S-net data. Human researchers interpreted the spatial and temporal relationships.
